concepts.name: Constitutional Status of ULBs: Before and After 74th Amendment
key_dimensions: Pre-1992 status: ULBs as a State subject under Entry 5, List II — no constitutional guarantee of existence
Post-74th Amendment: Addition of Part IX-A (Articles 243P–243ZG) and 12th Schedule to the Constitution
Distinction between 'constitutional status' and 'constitutional guarantee' — States can still dissolve ULBs
Comparison with 73rd Amendment (Panchayats) — structural parallels and key differences in scope

concepts.name: Definitions under Article 243P: Key Urban Terms
key_dimensions: Definition of 'Municipality', 'Metropolitan area' (population >10 lakh), 'District', and 'Local area'
Definition of 'Transitional area', 'Smaller urban area', 'Larger urban area' — criteria left to State Legislature
Trap: 'Metropolitan area' threshold is 10 lakh, not 1 lakh or 50 lakh — common confusion point
The term 'Ward' and 'Ward Committee' — trigger threshold (population >3 lakh for Ward Committees under Art. 243S)

concepts.name: Three Types of Municipalities under Article 243Q
key_dimensions: Nagar Panchayat (transitional area: rural to urban), Municipal Council (smaller urban area), Municipal Corporation (larger urban area)
Classification criteria are determined by the State Legislature — not fixed by the Constitution
Exception: Industrial townships under Article 243Q(2) — Governor may not constitute a Municipality if an industrial establishment provides services; UPSC trap on this exception
Overlap trap: Difference between a 'Nagar Panchayat' under 74th Amendment vs. informal usage of the term in different states

concepts.name: Composition and Ward System: Article 243R
key_dimensions: Direct election for all seats in a Municipality — seats filled by persons chosen by direct election from wards
Provision for representation of persons with special knowledge/experience in municipal administration — nominated, NOT with voting rights
Representation of MPs, MLAs, MLCs in Municipalities — with or without voting rights as State Legislature may provide
Trap: Nominated members (special knowledge) have NO voting rights; elected ward members have voting rights — a frequent MCQ trap

concepts.name: Reservation of Seats: Article 243T
key_dimensions: Mandatory reservation for SCs and STs in proportion to their population in the municipal area
Mandatory reservation of not less than one-third seats for women (including seats reserved for SC/ST women)
Reservation for OBCs: Not mandatory under the Constitution — left to the State Legislature (unlike SCs/STs); major UPSC trap
Rotation of reserved seats: Allotted by rotation to different constituencies — seats are not permanently reserved
Chairperson reservation: Article 243T(4) — reservation for SC, ST, and women in offices of Chairpersons as State Legislature may provide

concepts.name: Duration and Dissolution of Municipalities: Article 243U
key_dimensions: Fixed term of 5 years from the date of first meeting — dissolution before term requires due process
Mandatory elections BEFORE expiry of term; if dissolved, elections must be held within 6 months of dissolution
Reconstituted municipality after premature dissolution serves only the remainder of the original term, not a fresh 5 years
Trap: The 6-month rule for elections post-dissolution — similar to Article 174 (State Legislature sessions) but different context; also compare with 243E for Panchayats (identical provision)

concepts.name: State Election Commission: Article 243ZA (read with 243K)
key_dimensions: Superintendence, direction, and control of preparation of electoral rolls and conduct of elections vested in the State Election Commission
State Election Commissioner: appointed by Governor, removable only like a High Court judge — security of tenure
Trap: State Election Commission ≠ Election Commission of India; SECs are separate constitutional bodies for local body elections
State Legislature may make provisions for elections — but cannot divest superintendence from SEC; common controversy regarding delimitation

concepts.name: Powers and Functions: 12th Schedule (Article 243W)
key_dimensions: 18 functional items listed in the 12th Schedule — e.g., urban planning, land use regulation, public health, vital statistics, slum improvement, urban poverty alleviation
Critical trap: 12th Schedule lists are RECOMMENDATORY, not mandatory — States may or may not devolve these functions by law
Comparison with 11th Schedule (73rd Amendment, 29 items) — 74th has 18 items; both are enabling, not obligatory
High-yield items: Urban forestry (item 11), Regulation of slaughterhouses (item 12), Cattle pounds (item 13) — often appear in matching questions

concepts.name: Finance Commission for Municipalities: Article 243Y (read with 243I)
key_dimensions: Governor constitutes a State Finance Commission every 5 years to review financial position of Municipalities AND Panchayats
SFC recommends: distribution of taxes between State and Municipalities, grants-in-aid, measures to improve financial position
Distinction: State Finance Commission ≠ Finance Commission of India (Article 280); both can recommend local body grants but are separate bodies
Trap: The SFC covers BOTH rural (Panchayats) and urban (Municipalities) local bodies under Articles 243I and 243Y respectively — single body, dual mandate

concepts.name: Metropolitan Planning Committee: Article 243ZE
key_dimensions: Mandatory constitution of MPC for every Metropolitan area (population >10 lakh) — unlike DPC which is for every district
Composition: Not less than two-thirds of members elected from elected members of Municipalities and Panchayats in the Metropolitan area — in proportion to their population
MPC prepares a draft development plan for the Metropolitan area as a whole
Trap: MPC ≠ DPC (District Planning Committee under 243ZD); MPC is urban-metro specific, DPC is district-wide covering both rural and urban areas

concepts.name: District Planning Committee: Article 243ZD (Urban angle)
key_dimensions: Every State shall constitute a DPC to consolidate plans of Panchayats and Municipalities in the district
Composition: Not less than four-fifths members elected from elected members of Panchayats and Municipalities — proportional to rural/urban population
Chairperson of DPC forwards the development plan to the State Government

Trap: DPC creation is mandatory ('shall'), but in practice most states have not constituted them — question of constitutional compliance vs. political reality; also note DPC covers BOTH rural and urban unlike MPC

concepts.name: Ward Committees: Article 243S
key_dimensions: Mandatory constitution of Ward Committees in Municipalities with a population of 3 lakh or more
Composition and territorial area of Ward Committees determined by State Legislature
Trap: Ward Committees are mandatory only above 3 lakh population — below this threshold, States may constitute other committees at sub-municipal level
Ward Committees are participatory bodies at grassroots urban level — comparison with Gram Sabha in rural local governance (243A)

concepts.name: Exempted Areas: Article 243ZC
key_dimensions: Part IX-A does NOT apply to: Scheduled Areas referred to in Article 244(1), Tribal areas referred to in Article 244(2), Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council
Parliament may extend provisions to Scheduled/Tribal areas with exceptions and modifications
Trap: The exemption covers areas under 5th and 6th Schedules — PESA (1996) governs Panchayats in 5th Schedule areas but there is NO equivalent urban legislation for 6th Schedule tribal urban areas
Comparison with 243M (exemption for Panchayats) — similar structure but Darjeeling exemption explicitly mentioned only in 243ZC for ULBs

concepts.name: Disqualification of Members: Article 243V
key_dimensions: A person disqualified under State Legislature law for elections to the State Legislature is also disqualified for municipal elections
No person shall be disqualified on grounds of age if they have attained 21 years — minimum age for municipal membership is 21 (not 25 or 18)
Trap: Minimum age is 21 years for ULBs — same as Panchayats (243O); different from Lok Sabha (25) and Rajya Sabha (30)
Questions of disqualification decided by authority determined by the State Legislature — not by the Speaker or a court directly

concepts.name: Cantonment Boards and Their Exclusion from 74th Amendment
key_dimensions: Cantonment Boards are constituted under the Cantonments Act (originally 1924, now 2006) — a Central subject (Entry 3, List I)
Cantonment Boards are NOT covered by the 74th Amendment — they are not Municipalities under Part IX-A
Partial elected composition: Cantonment Boards have both elected and ex-officio (military) members — the Station Commander is the ex-officio President
Trap: Cantonment areas are urban areas but excluded from the municipal framework — a key overlap/exception question

concepts.name: Parastatal Bodies and the Problem of Functional Overlap
key_dimensions: Development authorities (e.g., DDA, BDA), Industrial Development Corporations, Housing Boards perform functions listed in 12th Schedule — bypassing elected ULBs
74th Amendment does not mandate dissolution of parastatal bodies — they coexist with ULBs, diluting municipal authority
Second ARC recommendation: Greater integration of parastatals with elected municipal bodies for unified urban governance
UPSC angle: This is the central critique of the 74th Amendment's implementation — devolution remains incomplete due to parallel bodies

concepts.name: Taxation Powers and Financial Autonomy of ULBs
key_dimensions: Article 243X: State Legislature may authorize a Municipality to levy, collect taxes, duties, tolls, fees; assign State taxes to Municipalities; provide grants-in-aid
Trap: Article 243X is enabling ('may'), not mandatory — unlike the clear mandate for SFC under 243Y; States are NOT obligated to devolve taxation powers
Own Source Revenue (OSR) of Indian ULBs is among the lowest globally (~1% of GDP) — governance and GS-II issue
Property tax as the primary own-source revenue for ULBs — reforms like GIS-based property tax, capital value system (Mumbai) as contemporary examples

concepts.name: Audit and Accounts: Article 243Z
key_dimensions: State Legislature may make provisions for maintenance of accounts and auditing of accounts of Municipalities
Trap: Article 243Z is again enabling ('may') — no mandatory CAG audit of municipal accounts prescribed in the Constitution (unlike Union/State accounts under Article 149)
CAG can audit ULBs only if entrusted by the Governor under Article 149 read with CAG Act — not automatic
Comparison: 73rd Amendment (Article 243J) has identical provision for Panchayat accounts — both are enabling, not mandatory

concepts.name: Smart Cities Mission and Constitutional Framework
key_dimensions: Smart Cities Mission (2015) operates through Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) — companies registered under Companies Act, not elected ULBs
Constitutional tension: SPVs bypass elected municipal councils, raising concerns about democratic accountability under Part IX-A
Functions of SPVs overlap with 12th Schedule items — urban planning, public health infrastructure, solid waste management
UPSC angle: Smart Cities vs. 74th Amendment — whether SPV model undermines constitutional intent of empowering elected ULBs; GS-II governance question

concepts.name: 15th Finance Commission Recommendations for Urban Local Bodies
key_dimensions: 15th FC recommended grants specifically tied to ULBs — divided into Basic Grants (untied) and Tied Grants (for sanitation/drinking water)
For the first time, grants to ULBs (and PRIs) made a direct constitutional recommendation under Article 280(3)(bb) — added by 73rd/74th Amendments
Conditionality for grants: States must publish audited accounts and notify floor rates for property tax — accountability mechanism
Trap: Article 280(3)(bb) was INSERTED by the 73rd/74th Amendments — the original Finance Commission under Article 280 did NOT cover local bodies; this is a frequently tested constitutional change
